We propose Gradient-Weighted Attention Attribution (GWAA), the first mechanistic credit assignment method for transformer-based RL agents. GWAA computes the gradient of the policy's log-probability with respect to the input embedding at each trajectory timestep and uses the resulting ℓ2-norm as a per-step saliency score, identifying the causal decision without requiring a language-model judge or reward model. We evaluate on stochastic FrozenLake-v1 using a behaviourally-cloned transformer agent and a novel slip-based ground-truth protocol: the causal step t * is the timestep at which environmental stochasticity deflected the agent into a danger zone, recorded with certainty by comparing intended versus actual state transitions. GWAA achieves Blame Precision@3 of 0.624 ± 0.031 versus 0.419 ± 0.007 for Reinforce with discounted returns (p = 0.004, Mann-Whitney U = 25, Cohen's d = 9.19, large effect), while adding zero overhead to the policy optimisation loop. We evaluate on stochastic FrozenLake-v1 using a behaviourally-cloned transformer agent and a novel slip-based ground-truth protocol: the causal step t * is the timestep at which environmental stochasticity deflected the agent into a danger zone, recorded with certainty by comparing intended versus actual state transitions. GWAA achieves Blame Precision@3 of 0.624 ± 0.031 versus 0.419 ± 0.007 for Reinforce with discounted returns (p = 0.004, Mann-Whitney U = 25, Cohen's d = 9.19, large effect), while adding zero overhead to the policy optimisation loop. An ablation over four transformer configurations confirms that deeper, wider attention stacks improve attribution precision monotonically.\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6843898\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.31234/osf.io/863eq\", \"title\": [\"Attribution of Responsibility Between Agents in a Causal Chain\"], \"abstract\": \"

When ordinary people hear about a `hired gun' killing, who do they judge to be more responsible -- the person who instigated the killing or the person who executed it? In this paper, we explored the attribution of causal and moral responsibility in a causal chain of events, where an agent A instructs an intermediate agent B to execute some harmful action which leads to a bad outcome to a victim V. In Study 1, participants judged B to be more of a cause, more blameworthy, and more deserving of punishment than A. In Study 2, we explored the effect of proximity by adding a third, subsequent contributing cause, such that B's action no longer as closely and directly caused the final bad outcome. Across three vignettes, participants judged both agents to be less causal, blameworthy, and deserving of punishment when they were less proximal to the outcome, but still judged B to be more morally and causally responsible than A in all conditions. In Study 3, we varied whether each of the two agents (A and B) intended for the final outcome to occur. We found an interaction between role and intent, where participants only mitigated causal and moral judgments for A when A did not intend for the outcome to occur -- regardless of B's intent. We discuss possible explanations for our findings and its implications for moral and legal decision-making.
